result.reason: The passage introduces Shmuel's teaching about selling a field without achrayut and asks 'what are the circumstances,' which is precisely what the 'Sale without Achrayut' section's prose describes as the opening of this discussion.

The passage presents both the 'other land' and 'no other land' scenarios as a single gemara unit asking 'heichi dami,' which the prose under 'Creditor Collection Cases' explicitly describes as the gemara's framework for examining both scenarios together.

Both items directly discuss the 'wicked borrower' (loveh rasha) rationale — item 1 introduces the answer that Reuven wants to avoid that status, and item 2 follows up with a challenge and response about whether he is equally a 'wicked borrower' toward the buyer — which is precisely what candidate 2 ('Non-Indebtedness Benefit') describes in its prose.

Both items together constitute Rava/Rav Pappa's announcement about the donkey seizure case and its immediate qualifications, which is precisely what the 'Reuven-Shimon-Marduk Case' prose introduces and discusses.

The passage is Ameimar's statement that even without any of the indicators, no obligation exists because gentiles are presumed extortionists, which is precisely what the 'Ameimar's Position' prose discusses.

The passage contains Rabba's exact qualification of the mishnah — that the craftsman has no chazakah only when delivery was witnessed, and that without witnesses the craftsman is believed via migo — which is precisely what the 'Rabba's View' section's prose describes.

The passage is Abaye's direct challenge to Rabba, arguing that even with witnesses the craftsman retains a migo via the claim 'I returned it to you' — exactly what the 'Abaye's Challenge' prose describes.
Both items are Rabba's direct response establishing that a deposit made with witnesses must be returned with witnesses — precisely the content described in the 'Return Requirement' prose.

The passage presents the full baraita including both the craftsman's failed claim and the third-party testimony clause, and the current heading's prose explicitly discusses both parts of this baraita as a unified unit under Abaye's meitivei objection.
Both items directly concern the latter clause (seifa) of the baraita and Rabba's migo-based explanation of why the third party is believed — exactly what the 'Third-Party Testimony' prose describes.

The passage presents Abaye's objection using the word 'ra'ah' from the baraita's first clause to challenge Rabba's witness-based position, which is precisely what the 'Eidim and Ra'ah' section's prose describes.

The passage contains Rabba's answer defending his position by specifying that witnesses are present AND ra'ah is required, which directly corresponds to the 'Combined Requirements' prose describing Rabba's third position that both eidim and ra'ah together are needed.
